newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian capital markets want privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian capital markets want privatisation.

text.p: Nigerian capital market operators on Friday urged government to sell off more state enterprises in 1997, saying privatisation would benefit the market.
Military ruler General Sani Abacha is due to broadcast the fiscal 1997 budget anytime from now on and the market expects him to announce further deregulation of one of Africa's biggest economies.
"We must push for government to stay out of businesses to enable private initiative take the leading role," said Femi Akinsanya, chief executive of securities firms Hamilton Hammer.
Akinsanya said he expected one or two parastatals or state-owned firms to be privatised in the course of the year.

"Privatisation is the most important thing for brokers. We expect a clear statement on what will be privatised in the next five to 10 years," said Aigboje Higo, head of brokerage house Counters Trust Securities Ltd.
He said government should put the most viable companies for sale first to generate good response.
Companies touted to go on the block include the state-owned airline as well as the electricity and telecoms concerns.
Analysts say this is what could attract foreign portfolio investors to the market.
Foreigners invested some $32 million in the Nigerian stock market in 1996 compared to $1.137 million a year earlier.
But operators say the figure would be higher when an automated clearing and settlement system becomes operational in the first quarter of 1997 after at least a year's delay.
"The CSCS (central securities and clearing system) is going to change trading," Azubuike Okpalaoka of TRW Stockbrokers said.
"It should also have a direct impact on velocity of transactions; it will speed things up," Akinsanya added.
Brokers expect the automated system to drastically cut the time spent on certification from several weeks to just three days, in line with the practice in advanced markets.
Analysts said reforms embarked upon by the Nigerian stock exchange in 1996 also buoyed activities, raising turnover and market capitalisation significantly.
Market capitalisation rose 70 percent to 285.6 billion naira in 1996 from 171.1 billion naira the year before. The all-share index was up by 37.3 percent in the same period.

Exchange officials attributed the impressive performances to share allocation system, more liberal pricing mechanism, reduced settlement period for transactions and a preferential system to speed up businesses for foreign investors.
They said a more stable foreign exchange and interest rate regime would also be good for the market. The dollar has been exchanging for 80 naira for most of 1996.
Nigeria has been in crisis since 1993 when the army annulled a presidential election presumed to have been won by businessman Moshood Abiola, a former chairman of the stock exchange.
The annulment strained relations with Western nations and traders said resolution of the political crisis would help restore confidence in Nigeria and boost business.
But they said they expected Abacha to preach reconciliation in his broadcast without announcing any new concrete steps to resolve the political crisis.
($1=80 naira)
